variants.title: Build the SFT dataset
variants.context: SFT data is built as an auditable dataset in four steps: collect representative failures with their metadata, write canonical responses under the production output contract, deduplicate and group related records, then freeze train, validation, and test splits. A random record-level split can place near-identical content on both sides of the evaluation boundary.
variants.prompt: A team is assembling its first fine-tuning dataset for a ticket-triage assistant. Put the dataset construction steps in order.

items.text: Freeze the train, validation, and test splits and keep the test set untouched until the release candidate is selected.
Cluster exact and near-duplicate records and keep the same user, source document, conversation, or incident in one split group.
Collect representative failures from real task shapes and edge cases, preserving source, permission, language, tenant, time, and difficulty metadata.
Write canonical responses under the production output contract and review factual support, policy behavior, and tool arguments.

variants.hint: Grouping happens before any split is drawn.
variants.explanation: Observe, label, isolate, then version. Deduplicating after the split lets paraphrases leak across the evaluation boundary.

variants.title: Build the SFT dataset
variants.context: SFT data is built as an auditable dataset in four steps: collect representative failures with their metadata, write canonical responses under the production output contract, deduplicate and group related records, then freeze train, validation, and test splits. A random record-level split can place near-identical content on both sides of the evaluation boundary.
variants.prompt: One support incident appears in the corpus as three paraphrased conversations. Put the steps in order so the incident cannot leak across the evaluation boundary.

items.text: Assign the whole incident cluster to one split group.
Cluster the three paraphrases as near duplicates of a single incident.
Write one canonical response per conversation under the output contract.
Sample the three conversations with their source and incident metadata intact.
Freeze the splits so the cluster lands entirely in train, validation, or test.

variants.hint: Which step guarantees that a paraphrase cannot end up on both sides?
variants.explanation: Near duplicates are clustered and grouped before splitting; otherwise memorizing one paraphrase looks like generalizing to another.

variants.title: Build the SFT dataset
variants.context: SFT data is built as an auditable dataset in four steps: collect representative failures with their metadata, write canonical responses under the production output contract, deduplicate and group related records, then freeze train, validation, and test splits. A random record-level split can place near-identical content on both sides of the evaluation boundary.
variants.prompt: Several checkpoints from one run are candidates for release. Put the steps in order from the dataset freeze to the final test measurement.

items.text: Select the release candidate from the validation evidence.
Freeze the train, validation, and test splits with their split groups versioned.
Compare the checkpoints and hyperparameters on the validation split only.
Measure the selected candidate once on the untouched test split.
Train the run and save several checkpoints against the frozen training split.

variants.hint: Which split is allowed to influence the checkpoint choice?
variants.explanation: Validation drives checkpoint and hyperparameter choices; the test set stays untouched until the release candidate is already selected.

variants.title: Ship and roll back
variants.context: Rollout starts with offline replay, then shadow or canary traffic compared against the stable release on the same traffic distribution, with automatic stops on critical failures. Rollback moves a versioned alias to the previous complete manifest and restores the matching base, tokenizer, template, prompt, safety policy, and runtime.
variants.prompt: A fine-tuned checkpoint has passed its release gates. Put the rollout steps in order, starting from the release contract.

items.text: Compare the candidate against the stable release on the same traffic distribution.
Define canary exposure, stop conditions, owners, and the immutable rollback manifest in the release contract.
Send shadow or canary traffic appropriate to the data policy.
Replay the candidate offline against recorded traffic.
Stop exposure automatically when a critical safety, correctness, latency, or compatibility failure appears.

variants.hint: Stop conditions are written down before any traffic is exposed.
variants.explanation: Offline replay precedes live exposure, and exposure grows only under predeclared stop conditions with a rollback target already named.

variants.title: Ship and roll back
variants.context: Rollout starts with offline replay, then shadow or canary traffic compared against the stable release on the same traffic distribution, with automatic stops on critical failures. Rollback moves a versioned alias to the previous complete manifest and restores the matching base, tokenizer, template, prompt, safety policy, and runtime.
variants.prompt: A canary shows a spike in unsupported claims. Put the rollback steps in order.

items.text: Restore the matching base, tokenizer, template, prompt, safety policy, and runtime.
Decide whether to retrain from the measured failure cluster rather than the calendar.
Move the versioned alias to the previous complete manifest.
Preserve bounded evidence for incident analysis without retaining unnecessary sensitive text.
The predeclared stop condition halts canary exposure automatically.

variants.hint: Rollback restores a whole configuration, not a single weight file.
variants.explanation: Stop, restore the previous manifest as a complete configuration, keep bounded evidence, and let the measured failure cluster drive the next training decision.

variants.title: Ship and roll back
variants.context: Rollout starts with offline replay, then shadow or canary traffic compared against the stable release on the same traffic distribution, with automatic stops on critical failures. Rollback moves a versioned alias to the previous complete manifest and restores the matching base, tokenizer, template, prompt, safety policy, and runtime.
variants.prompt: A LoRA adapter is merged into a full checkpoint for a simpler runtime. Put the steps in order from the merge to live traffic.

items.text: Replay the merged artifact offline before any live exposure.
Record the merged artifact in an immutable manifest with the previous stable alias as its rollback target.
Merge the adapter into a new full checkpoint in a controlled build.
Re-run serialization, generation parity, latency, memory, safety, and rollback checks on the merged artifact.
Canary it against the stable release and stop automatically on critical failures.

variants.hint: A merge produces a new artifact that has not yet earned any release evidence.
variants.explanation: Merging produces a new full checkpoint, so it repeats the checks, the manifest, the offline replay, and the canary like any other release.

variants.title: Do the batch math
variants.context: Effective batch size is microbatch times gradient accumulation times data-parallel workers. Raising it changes gradient noise and the number of optimizer updates per epoch, so it is not only a memory workaround.
variants.prompt: A run uses a microbatch of 4 sequences, 8 gradient accumulation steps, and 4 data-parallel workers. What is the effective batch size?
variants.explanation: 4 x 8 x 4 = 128 sequences contribute to each optimizer update.

mistakes.feedback: You multiplied microbatch by accumulation but left out the data-parallel workers.
The three factors multiply; they do not add.

variants.title: Do the batch math
variants.context: Effective batch size is microbatch times gradient accumulation times data-parallel workers. Raising it changes gradient noise and the number of optimizer updates per epoch, so it is not only a memory workaround.
variants.prompt: The release contract calls for an effective batch of 256 sequences. Each worker fits a microbatch of 2, and there are 8 workers. How many gradient accumulation steps are needed?
variants.hint: Divide the target by what one step already covers across all workers.

mistakes.feedback: Divide by microbatch and workers together, not by the microbatch alone.
Divide by microbatch and workers together, not by the workers alone.

variants.title: Do the batch math
variants.context: Effective batch size is microbatch times gradient accumulation times data-parallel workers. Raising it changes gradient noise and the number of optimizer updates per epoch, so it is not only a memory workaround.
variants.prompt: The training set holds 25,600 records. The team raises gradient accumulation from 4 to 8 while keeping a microbatch of 4 on 4 workers. How many optimizer updates happen per epoch after the change?
variants.hint: Recompute the effective batch first, then divide the record count by it.
variants.explanation: The effective batch doubles from 64 to 128, so 25,600 / 128 = 200 updates per epoch instead of 400.

mistakes.feedback: That is the count before the change; the effective batch doubled to 128.
Divide by the full effective batch of 128, not by microbatch times workers.

variants.title: Pick the smallest intervention
variants.context: Start with the failure, not the training method. Prompting with schemas, examples, and validators when the base model can already perform the task; retrieval when answers depend on private, changing, or attributable facts; a LoRA adapter when a measured behavior gap remains and a reversible artifact is valuable; full fine-tuning only when evaluation evidence justifies the larger compute, storage, and release surface.
variants.prompt: In manual tests a base model assigns the correct triage labels but returns them in inconsistent JSON shapes. The prompt has no schema, examples, or validator yet. What is the first experiment?
options: Add a schema, examples, and an output validator to the prompt and measure again.
Train a LoRA adapter on 2,000 labeled tickets to stabilize the format.
Run full fine-tuning so the format holds across every future version.
optionFeedback: The base model already performs the task, so the cheapest intervention that can pass the eval comes first.
An adapter is justified only after a measured behavior gap survives better prompting.
Full fine-tuning is the largest release surface and needs evidence that smaller methods failed.
variants.hint: Can the base model already do the task?
variants.explanation: Choose the least expensive method that can falsify the hypothesis; prompting is tried before any training.

variants.title: Pick the smallest intervention
variants.context: Start with the failure, not the training method. Prompting with schemas, examples, and validators when the base model can already perform the task; retrieval when answers depend on private, changing, or attributable facts; a LoRA adapter when a measured behavior gap remains and a reversible artifact is valuable; full fine-tuning only when evaluation evidence justifies the larger compute, storage, and release surface.
variants.prompt: After the strongest prompt-only baseline, a measured 14-point gap remains on refusal style, and the team wants to switch the behavior on per tenant and roll it back cheaply. Which intervention fits?
options: Full-parameter fine-tuning of the base model on the style examples.
Retrieval over the style guide so the model reads the rules at request time.
A LoRA adapter trained on the behavior and versioned with its base and template.
optionFeedback: Full fine-tuning multiplies storage and rollback cost and cannot be swapped per tenant cheaply.
Retrieval supplies current facts and evidence; it does not make a behavior practiced across many examples.
A measured gap plus the need for a small, reversible, swappable artifact is the adapter case.
variants.hint: Which method yields a small, reversible task artifact?
variants.explanation: Train a small adapter when a measured behavior gap remains and a reversible task artifact is valuable.

variants.title: Pick the smallest intervention
variants.context: Start with the failure, not the training method. Prompting with schemas, examples, and validators when the base model can already perform the task; retrieval when answers depend on private, changing, or attributable facts; a LoRA adapter when a measured behavior gap remains and a reversible artifact is valuable; full fine-tuning only when evaluation evidence justifies the larger compute, storage, and release surface.
variants.prompt: A PEFT run beats the prompt baseline. One engineer says this proves full SFT will never be needed; another says full SFT should ship anyway because it won a public benchmark. Who is right?
options: The first engineer; a PEFT win retires full SFT for this task.
The second engineer; a benchmark win pays for the production cost.
Neither; each claim needs a controlled comparison on this task's evidence and cost.
optionFeedback: A PEFT win does not prove full SFT is unnecessary forever.
A full-SFT win on one benchmark does not justify its production cost automatically.
Both methods must be compared on the same held-out cases with their operational surface counted.
variants.hint: What kind of evidence does the lesson accept for a method choice?
variants.explanation: Start with the least expensive method that can falsify the hypothesis, and treat each further step as its own controlled comparison.

variants.title: Judge the release evidence
variants.context: A candidate releases only when quality, rare slices, safety, regression, lineage, artifact support, and rollback all pass as independent gates declared before training. The formatting contract must be identical between training and serving, and model-based graders need their own validation, calibration, and versioning.
variants.prompt: The team trained first, saw the candidate reach 91 percent aggregate quality, and then set the release threshold at 90 percent. What is wrong?
options: The threshold should be raised to 95 percent to be safe.
The gate was chosen after seeing the candidate, so it is not a gate.
optionFeedback: Raising the number afterwards is still choosing it after the fact.
A threshold picked after the result is known cannot fail the candidate.
Aggregate and slice gates are declared before training.
variants.explanation: Declare aggregate and slice gates before training; do not choose thresholds after seeing the candidate.

variants.title: Judge the release evidence
variants.context: A candidate releases only when quality, rare slices, safety, regression, lineage, artifact support, and rollback all pass as independent gates declared before training. The formatting contract must be identical between training and serving, and model-based graders need their own validation, calibration, and versioning.
variants.prompt: Serving upgrades the chat template to new role markers. The adapter trained on the old template is loaded unchanged and aggregate quality still passes. What should the lineage gate do?
options: Reject it; a template change alters the token sequence the adapter learned.
Allow it; the adapter weights themselves did not change.
Allow it; the aggregate score already covers the change.
optionFeedback: The formatting contract spans training and serving; the adapter is bound to its template.
A visually similar conversation becomes a different token sequence when a boundary changes.
Lineage is an independent gate, and an aggregate score can hide a formatting mismatch.
variants.hint: Is an adapter a portable behavior file?
variants.explanation: A LoRA adapter trained against one base checkpoint or chat template is not portable; the same template must be replayed in serving.

variants.title: Judge the release evidence
variants.context: A candidate releases only when quality, rare slices, safety, regression, lineage, artifact support, and rollback all pass as independent gates declared before training. The formatting contract must be identical between training and serving, and model-based graders need their own validation, calibration, and versioning.
variants.prompt: A model-based grader scores the candidate 9 points above the base model. The team wants to release on that number. Is it sufficient release evidence?
options: Only if the grader is validated and calibrated, with regressions reported separately.
No; only blinded human review counts as release evidence.
Yes, as long as the grader is a larger model than the candidate.
optionFeedback: Graders are instruments that must be validated, and aggregate gains cannot hide separate regressions.
Human review is required where the rubric is subjective, but validated graders remain useful evidence.
Grader size is not validation; the grader needs its own calibration evidence.
variants.hint: What must be true of the measuring instrument itself?
variants.explanation: Model-based graders need their own validation, calibration, and versioning, and safety regressions stay separate from aggregate improvement.
